Comet is Perplexity's free web browser with an AI assistant built in.
Open it on any page to summarize, explain or compare, or give it a task.
Use it with care: researchers showed hidden text on a page could steer the assistant.

Would you let a browser shop for you?

threads_text: Perplexity's Comet browser is free and has an assistant that can summarize any page or do tasks like comparing prices across stores. Security researchers showed hidden text on a page could steer it, so the last click should stay yours. Would you let a browser shop for you?

slides.headline: How to use *Comet*, Perplexity's free AI browser

slides.heading: 1. *Import* your old browser
paras: Menu (three dots), Settings, then Import bookmarks and settings.
Pick your old browser and choose bookmarks, history or passwords. Most Chrome extensions work.

slides.heading: 2. Open the *assistant*
paras: Open it as a side panel on any page and ask about what you see.
Alt + S summarizes the page. Alt + Shift + V starts voice mode.

slides.heading: 3. Keep the *last click*
paras: Brave showed hidden text on a page could give the assistant orders.
Let it compare and fill forms, but pay, send and sign yourself.

site_article.headline: How to use Comet browser: Perplexity's free AI browser, step by step
site_article.dek: Comet puts an AI assistant inside your browser. Here is how to set it up, the shortcuts and prompts that matter, and where to be careful.
site_article.summary: Comet is Perplexity's free web browser with a built-in AI assistant that can summarize pages, answer questions about them and carry out tasks. It runs on Windows, Mac, Android and iPhone.
site_article.seo_title: How to use Comet browser: Perplexity's AI browser guide
site_article.seo_description: How to use Comet browser: install it, import from Chrome, open the assistant, shortcuts, 5 prompts to copy and how to stay safe with its agent.
site_article.answer_summary: To use Comet, download it for Windows or Mac (or the Android or iPhone app), import your bookmarks from Settings, then open the Comet Assistant on any page to summarize it, ask about it or give it a task. Comet has been free since October 2025.
site_article.hero_alt: Perplexity's Comet browser app in use on a phone.

paragraphs.text: How to use Comet browser, in short: install it, bring over your bookmarks and passwords, then open the Comet Assistant on any page and ask it to summarize, explain or do a task for you. Comet is Perplexity's web browser with an AI assistant built in, and Perplexity says the assistant can run multi-step tasks from a plain request while keeping track of what you are doing.

It costs nothing to start. Perplexity made Comet free for everyone in October 2025, after launching it in July 2025 for subscribers to its top Max plan. It runs on Windows and Mac, and there are also apps for Android, released in November 2025, and for iPhone, released in March 2026.
How to install Comet and import from Chrome

paragraphs.title: 1. Download it
paragraphs.text: Get Comet from the official Comet website and choose the Windows or Mac version. On a Mac, drag the Comet icon into Applications. On Windows, run the installer and follow the prompts. Comet opens on its own when the install finishes. On a phone, install it from the Play Store or the App Store.

paragraphs.title: 2. Bring your old browser with you
paragraphs.text: Click the menu button (three dots) in the top right corner, go to Settings and choose Import bookmarks and settings. Pick your old browser from the list, tick what you want (bookmarks, history, passwords) and click Import. Perplexity's help center says most Chrome extensions work in Comet too.

paragraphs.title: 3. Sign in
paragraphs.text: Signing in to your Perplexity account is optional, but Tom's Guide recommends it. Updates install when you relaunch the browser, and you can check for one under Settings, then About.

Comet asks for access to your Mac keychain during setup. Perplexity's help center says it uses it to store passwords, autofill payment details and data for its personal features, encrypted on your device. If that makes you uneasy, skip the password import and keep your passwords where they are.
How to use the Comet Assistant

The assistant is the reason to switch. Comet's home page opens as a chat, and on any website you can open the assistant as a side panel, according to TechRadar. It can see the page you are on, so you can ask about it without copying anything.

paragraphs.title: 4. Summarize a long page
paragraphs.text: Click the Summarize button, or press Alt + S, according to Tom's Guide. On Android, Comet can summarize all your open tabs at once, not only the one in front of you.

paragraphs.title: 5. Ask about what you are reading
paragraphs.text: Highlight a passage and ask what it means, or use the Ask button for context on the page. This is the fastest way through a contract, a research paper or a long product page.

paragraphs.title: 6. Talk to it
paragraphs.text: Click the waveform icon in the top right corner, or press Alt + Shift + V, to use voice mode, according to Tom's Guide. On Android, Perplexity says you can talk to the assistant to find something across all your open tabs.

paragraphs.title: 7. Give it a task
paragraphs.text: Ask the assistant to do something, not just answer. Perplexity's own examples include finding other sites that sell the same bike with faster shipping, comparing insurance plans and booking a meeting based on something you just read. On Android, the assistant shows each action it takes, and you can step in at any time.
5 Comet prompts to copy

paragraphs.title: Prompt 1: Get the short version
paragraphs.text: Summarize this page in 5 bullet points. Then tell me the one thing the author wants me to do or believe.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 2: Compare before you buy
paragraphs.text: Find 3 other stores that sell this exact product. Show the price, shipping time and return policy for each in a table. Do not buy anything.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 3: Clean up your tabs
paragraphs.text: Group my open tabs by topic and tell me which ones look like duplicates.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 4: Study mode
paragraphs.text: Read this chapter and quiz me with 5 questions, one at a time. Tell me if I got each one right before you ask the next.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 5: Plan a dinner, stop before paying
paragraphs.text: Find a table for two at an Italian restaurant near [your neighborhood] for Friday at 7 pm. Show me the options and wait for me to pick one.
Prompt 4 is not a trick: Android Central reports that Comet can read an online textbook and quiz you on it, and that it can shop for you within a price range and at a retailer you name.
What Comet is good at, and where it falls short

In TechRadar's test, Comet built a two month events calendar from the reviewer's Google account in a couple of minutes, and on a grocery site it filled in his details, picked the ingredients for a recipe and left the order waiting for him to confirm. The same reviewer saw some lag and sometimes had to explain a request again.

The bigger issue is safety. In August 2025, Brave showed that hidden text on a web page, such as a Reddit comment, could give Comet's assistant instructions when a user asked it to summarize that page. In Brave's demo, those hidden instructions led the assistant to the user's email and a login code. Brave later wrote that the issue was not fully fixed and that it had reported it again.

Engadget, writing about the iPhone app, advised caution with shopping and scheduling tasks because AI browsers can fall for online scams. It also noted that the iPhone app does not support third-party extensions and that Perplexity has said it uses its browser partly to collect data for ad targeting.
Keep the agent away from anything you cannot undo. Use it on pages you trust, read what it plans to do before it acts, and do the final click yourself on payments, emails and account settings.

Comet is worth installing if you read a lot online and want summaries and comparisons without copying text into a chatbot. It is less convincing as a hands-off shopping or booking agent: the tests show it works, but the security research is a good reason to keep a human on the last step.
